text: Around 2,000 years ago, ships sailed from Egypt to India's southern coast, riding the
monsoon winds.
They went home, loaded with pepper, gems, and cotton cloth.
And Rome paid in gold.
So much gold that the Roman writer Pliny complained about it.
He grumbled that India drained the empire of 50 million sesterces every single year.
Hoards of Roman coins still turn up in South India today.
Keep Pliny's complaint in mind, 17 centuries later, someone in India is going to make exactly
the same complaint.
The other way round.
In the north, newcomers from Central Asia, the Kushans, built an empire, and their greatest
king became a champion of Buddhism.
Remember our question?
They came as outsiders, they stayed, and became part of India.
Then, around 320 CE, a new family united the north, the Gupta's.
And what people remember about the Gupta age isn't its battles, it's its ideas.
In 499, a 23-year-old mathematician named Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins on its
own axis.
That's about a thousand years before Copernicus.
So, the sky turns around the Earth every night?
No.
Now, the Earth turns, the skies stay still.
Then why am I not dizzy?
I'll explain tomorrow, if the Earth is still here.
Aryabhata also worked out pi to four decimal places, 3.1416, and Indian mathematicians were
building the number system you use every single day.
Nine digits plus a sign for nothing.
A little later, another mathematician wrote down the rules for zero as a number in its
own right.
Those numerals traveled to the Arab world and then to Europe, which is why Europeans
called them Arabic numerals.
The numbers on your phone are Indian.
This age gave the world something else, too.
A war game on an 8x8 board with elephants, chariots, horses, and foot soldiers.
Chaturanga. Carried west through Persia, it became the game we call chess. Students crossed
Asia to study at Nalanda, one of the world's first great universities. And in Delhi stands
an iron pillar from this age that has stood in the rain for about 1,600 years and has barely rusted.
In the far south, the Chola kings later built one of the greatest navies in Asian history
and sent it across the sea to attack kingdoms in Sumatra and Malaya.
This was the land Indians still call, in its richest times, Soni Kichiriya, the Golden
Bird.
And a bird that shiny gets noticed.
In Afghanistan, a powerful sultan had just learned exactly how much gold was sitting
inside India's temples.
